<content>
1: # Over-constrain, and read the violation
2: 
3: A passing timing constraint establishes closure at the tested target and conditions. Preserve the
4: actual reported slack, whether zero or positive. Some synthesis flows report zero once a target is
5: met; that zero does not establish the fastest achievable implementation. A pass alone does not
6: prove global optimality, and a negative slack does not prove the tool exhausted every strategy.
7: 
8: A setup violation is a measured shortfall. For an asked period P and slack V < 0, P + |V| can guide
9: the next trial when the timing model makes that approximation useful. It remains a hypothesis:
10: resynthesis, path changes, and period-dependent IO delays or clock latency can change the result.
11: Only a new valid trial can establish closure at its tested period.
12: 
13: ## What this means for a Pack
14: 
15: - Keep the requested target, reported clock period, actual slack and proposed next target distinct.
16:   Check the report's units, scope and conditions before using it in a decision.
17: - A deliberately tighter first trial can expose a shortfall; a passing trial is still useful
18:   evidence. Choose the initial pressure from the business question and available budget.
19: - A Pack may recommend `P + |V| - step` after failure and `P - step` after a passing trial that
20:   misses Goal. Do not systematically relax a zero-slack passing trial by adding a guard band.
21:   Validate every candidate against the Pack's bounds and precision before launching it.
22: - Use the tool's actual reporting precision. Repeated rounded values can hide differences;
23:   convergence is limited to the observed resolution and tested conditions.
24: - State: “Trial X measured slack Y; the next proposed period is Z and remains untested.”
25:   Claim Goal met only from current, valid measurements and the required Judge verdicts.
26: - Execution faults, incomplete reports and changed inputs cannot support a design conclusion.
27:   Retain the failure and resolve it before deriving the next strategy.
28: 
29: ## Source and limits
30: 
31: The reference opene902 stand-in exposed a chooser that relaxed the period on every zero-slack pass.
32: That counterexample motivated the over-constraining recommendation. It does not establish that
33: all tools always report zero, or that one failed synthesis reveals the exact achievable period.
34: When citing this file, identify the recommendation used and the actual evidence behind the decision.

(End of file - total 34 lines)
</content>

<path>/private/tmp/hima-l4-AT8h3n/hima-home-OzRhpJ/profiles/hima/node_modules/@hima/harness/skills/knowledge/end-honestly-in-more-than-one-way.md</path>
<type>file</type>
<content>
1: # End honestly, and in more than one way
2: 
3: A Campaign ends in facts. There are exactly three honest ways for one to end, and a generation limit
4: is not among them.
5: 
6: 1. **The Goal is met.** The target was reached and the constraints hold, stated with the values and
7:    the citations that say so.
8: 2. **The exploration converged.** The moves stopped changing anything: the value the Loop converges
9:    on stayed inside the declared band across the declared number of generations. "Converged" is a
10:    measurement, not a mood — the pack declares which value and which band.
11: 3. **An ending the pack declares in its own words.** Something in the business said stop, and the
12:    pack said in advance what that would be: a gate the library tool refuses to pass, adoption that
13:    stayed at zero, an input the flow rejects, a stage that cannot run on this Site at all.
14: 
15: **A generation limit is a budget, not an ending.** When a Campaign stops because it ran out of
16: generations, nobody knows what happened: the method may have been converging slowly, or it may have
17: been walking away from the answer for its whole life. An ending nobody can explain is the one thing a
18: Campaign must not deliver, because the whole promise is that it ends in facts.
19: 
20: ## What this means for a pack you are authoring
21: 
22: - **Write the `Endings` section first, not last.** Every way this business can stop, in the words a
23:   person would use. If you cannot name three, you do not yet know the business well enough to author
24:   the pack.
25: - **Every declared ending needs the value that detects it.** An ending that no reader produces a
26:   number for is an ending the runner can never reach. If the pack says "stop when the library gate
27:   fails", some reader has to report whether the gate failed.
28: - **Convergence is stated in the chooser's own vocabulary.** The value converged on has to be one
29:   the chooser actually reads; a pack that converges on a number its chooser never looks at can only
30:   ever end at its limit.
31: - **The generation limit stays, and stays a budget.** It protects the Site and the person's time. It
32:   should be reached only when something is wrong, and when it is reached the report says so plainly
33:   rather than dressing it up as a conclusion.
34: - **Say what a person must never have to guess.** If a stop can be read two ways — met exactly, or
35:   not measured at all — the pack's words must distinguish them on every face.
36: 
37: ## Citing it
38: 
39: When this file shaped a decision, cite it by name and say what it changed — "made every ending one
40: this pack declares in words, and added the reader that detects the library gate's refusal".

(End of file - total 40 lines)
</content>

<path>/private/tmp/hima-l4-AT8h3n/hima-home-OzRhpJ/profiles/hima/node_modules/@hima/harness/skills/knowledge/assert-the-checker-options.md</path>
<type>file</type>
<content>
1: # Assert the verification tool's options before the run counts
2: 
3: A verification session answers the question its options asked, not the question you meant. The same
4: tool, on the same data, with a different rule deck, a different cell view, a different set of checks
5: enabled or a different severity threshold, will answer "clean" and "not clean" with equal confidence
6: — and both answers are correct for what was actually asked.
7: 
8: **So a run whose options were not asserted has not verified anything.** It has produced a number
9: whose meaning nobody can state afterwards, and a pass obtained under the wrong options is worse than
10: a failure: it is a failure that looks like success and travels into a report as a fact.
11: 
12: ## What this means for a pack you are authoring
13: 
14: - **Declare the options in the pack, beside the constraint they serve.** Which checks, which rule
15:   set, which views, which thresholds. Not "the usual ones" — the list, written down.
16: - **Assert them at run time, before the count is read.** The session must be made to state the
17:   options it ran under, and a reader must hold that statement against the declaration. If the two
18:   disagree, the generation has no verdict: it has a blocker, and the pack says so in words.
19: - **Make the assertion a typed value, not a comment.** "Options as declared: yes/no", plus the list
20:   the session reported, so the judge can cite it and a person reading the report six months later can
21:   see exactly what was checked.
22: - **Never infer the options from the result.** A clean result is not evidence that the right checks
23:   ran; it is equally consistent with no checks having run at all.
24: - **Record the tool's own version beside them.** Options mean different things across versions, and a
25:   Campaign compared against an earlier one has to be able to say whether that comparison is fair.
26: 
27: ## The failure this prevents
28: 
29: A generation passes; the report says the design is clean; the option set had one whole class of check
30: switched off. Nothing in the ledger is wrong — every number is what the tool said — and the
31: conclusion is false. There is no way to detect this later from the numbers alone, which is why the
32: assertion has to happen before the count is read rather than after the campaign is over.
33: 
34: ## Citing it
35: 
36: When this file shaped a decision, cite it by name and say what it changed — "added the declared
37: option list to the run contract and an assertion reader that fails the generation when the session
38: reports anything else".

(End of file - total 38 lines)
</content>

<path>/private/tmp/hima-l4-AT8h3n/hima-home-OzRhpJ/profiles/hima/node_modules/@hima/harness/skills/knowledge/one-checker-per-session.md</path>
<type>file</type>
<content>
1: # One verification tool per session
2: 
3: A count belongs to one tool and one option set. Run two verification tools in one session and the
4: violation count that comes out belongs to neither: you cannot say which tool found what, you cannot
5: compare the number against a run of either tool alone, and you cannot re-run half of it.
6: 
7: **So a session runs one verification tool.** Not one *kind* of tool — one tool. If the business needs
8: two, that is two act nodes, two sessions, two reports and two typed values.
9: 
10: ## What this means for a pack you are authoring
11: 
12: - **One act node per verification tool.** Each node launches its own session, produces its own
13:   report, and its report is read by its own reader into its own named value. The node's name says
14:   which tool it is.
15: - **Name the values after what produced them.** Two values both called "violations" will be compared
16:   by somebody. Give each the tool's name in its own name, and its unit and meaning in the pack's
17:   `Semantics`.
18: - **Do not sum across tools.** A total over two tools' counts is a number with no unit and no owner.
19:   If the business wants one verdict, the judge takes it from a rule over the two named values, and
20:   the rule says in words how the two combine.
21: - **Fork rather than fold.** Two verification tools that can run at once are two branches of a fork
22:   that converge into a judge node — that is what fork and join are for, and it keeps each count
23:   attached to the session that produced it.
24: - **One session, one option set.** The companion rule is in `assert-the-checker-options.md`: a
25:   session whose options were not asserted has verified nothing, and a session running two tools
26:   cannot have one asserted option set at all.
27: 
28: ## The failure this prevents
29: 
30: A single session runs two tools to save a licence checkout; the report carries one count; six months
31: later a person asks which tool found the seventeen violations and no record can answer. The Campaign
32: ended in a number rather than in facts.
33: 
34: ## Citing it
35: 
36: When this file shaped a decision, cite it by name and say what it changed — "split the one
37: verification node into two, one per tool, each with its own reader and its own named count, joined at
38: a judge node".

(End of file - total 38 lines)
</content>

<path>/private/tmp/hima-l4-AT8h3n/hima-home-OzRhpJ/profiles/hima/node_modules/@hima/harness/skills/knowledge/attribute-by-database-relation.md</path>
<type>file</type>
<content>
1: # Attribute adoption through the database relation, never through a name
2: 
3: When a campaign asks "was this thing actually used?", the answer lives in the tool's own database, in
4: the relation between an instance and the master it was built from. Ask the database for that
5: relation and you get the truth the tool itself acts on.
6: 
7: **Do not answer it by matching names.** Grepping a netlist for a prefix, counting lines whose text
8: looks right, or matching a naming convention answers a different question — "does this text appear?"
9: — and it is wrong in both directions:
10: 
11: - **False positives.** A name that merely resembles the convention is counted. Text in a comment, a
12:   hierarchical path that contains the prefix on its way somewhere else, an instance that was created
13:   and then optimized away but still appears in an earlier section of the file.
14: - **False negatives.** The tool renamed, uniquified, folded or buffered the instance, and the name
15:   that survives no longer matches anything. Everything you were looking for is there and you count
16:   zero.
17: 
18: And names are a convention. Conventions change between tool versions, between flows, and between the
19: person who set them up and the person running the campaign today.
20: 
21: ## What this means for a pack you are authoring
22: 
23: - **Read adoption from the tool database, through the instance-to-master relation.** The act node
24:   runs the tool's own query; the reader reads that query's output into a typed value. Its `Semantics`
25:   entry says what the relation is, not what the name looks like.
26: - **Report the denominator too.** "Forty instances adopted" is not a measurement; "forty of two
27:   hundred and ten instances" is. The chooser and the judge both need the ratio, and a person reading
28:   the report needs to know what it is out of.
29: - **If a database query is impossible, say so in the pack rather than substituting a grep.** A pack
30:   that cannot measure adoption honestly declares that as one of its endings; it does not report a
31:   number it does not believe.
32: - **Never let a name-match become the fallback path.** A reader that queries the database and falls
33:   back to matching names when the query fails will fall back silently, one day, and the campaign will
34:   end on a number nobody can account for. A failed query is a blocker with the query in it.
35: 
36: ## Citing it
37: 
38: When this file shaped a decision, cite it by name and say what it changed — "made the adoption reader
39: run the tool's own instance-to-master query and report both the count and its denominator, and made a
40: failed query a blocker rather than a zero".

(End of file - total 40 lines)
</content>

<path>/private/tmp/hima-l4-AT8h3n/hima-home-OzRhpJ/profiles/hima/node_modules/@hima/harness/skills/knowledge/what-a-golden-flow-is.md</path>

<content>
1: # What a Golden Flow is
2: 
3: **The Golden Flow is the reference engineering flow a HimaPack is learned from and checked against:
4: how the business runs in real tools on a real Site.** That is the whole of the definition, and every
5: clause of it does work.
6: 
7: - **Learned from.** You read it to find out what the business actually does: which stages exist,
8:   which of them produce the numbers the business cares about, which knobs a stage takes and where it
9:   takes them from, what the reports look like, what has to be true before a stage can run.
10: - **Checked against.** When the pack runs, its results are held against what the flow does. A pack
11:   whose campaign cannot be compared to the reference has not been tested.
12: - **Reference material, never the goal.** Reproducing the flow is not the objective. The pack's
13:   objective is the business's — a target and its constraints. The flow is how you learn what that
14:   means in practice.
15: - **Never imported.** Not one file of it is copied into the pack folder. A pack is a portable method
16:   that binds to any Site meeting its contract; a pack carrying a copy of one Site's flow is a pack
17:   that has silently become that Site's. The pack records **where the flow lies** and **what was read
18:   there**, as pointers.
19: 
20: ## What this means for a pack you are authoring
21: 
22: - **Read it where it lies, with read tools.** Ask the author for the path. Read the flow's own build
23:   file first: it names the stages and the variables each one takes, and a variable a stage takes on
24:   the command line is a knob a generation can set without editing anything.
25: - **Write down pointers, not contents.** "`<flowRoot>/Makefile` — the stages, and the variables each
26:   takes" is a pointer. A pasted copy of the file is an import, and it goes stale the first time
27:   somebody edits the real one.
28: - **Raise every disagreement as its own question.** Where the author's words and the flow differ,
29:   neither side wins silently: the flow may be doing something the author has forgotten, and the
30:   author may know something the flow does not encode. Ask, and record how it was settled.
31: - **The harness copies the flow for a run; you do not copy it for the pack.** A Campaign's workspace
32:   preparation makes its own copy of the pieces the contract names, so a generation never writes into
33:   the reference. That is the runner's job and it is already done.
34: - **A flow that cannot be read is a stop, not a guess.** If the author cannot say where it lies, or
35:   the path is not readable, say so and stop. A pack authored from a description of a flow nobody
36:   looked at is a pack of guesses.
37: 
38: ## Citing it
39: 
40: When this file shaped a decision, cite it by name and say what it changed — "kept the flow where it
41: lies: the record carries the path and what was read there, and no file of it was copied into the
42: pack".

(End of file - total 42 lines)
</content>

1: ## Business
2: 
3: **Scope, stated once and repeated in the specification and the test record.** This Pack performs one bounded local authoring-qualification check of one local JSON input, and nothing else. It checks only that a source contract was present and read. It does not invoke Liberty, does not invoke QuaLib, does not call `edarun`, uses no production Library facts, requalifies no Wave 2 E1--E4 method, touches no customer data, and therefore claims no commercial qualification. A PASS is not qualification of any Library. The customer-facing wording must say that native QuaLib qualification, production Library facts and Wave 2 E1--E4 claims are outside this Pack's TEST.
4: 
5: **What is explored.** Nothing varies. One generation re-runs the same fixed input through the same two commands; the flow exposes no knob that changes what is checked. The input is one JSON file and its 64-hex `sourceSha256`, fixed before the Run and immutable for it, so a different input is a new Campaign rather than a second generation. The unit of exploration is therefore the single bounded contract check itself, not a swept or stepped quantity.
6: 
7: **What is measured.** Exactly one reading: `library_contract_ready`, unit `count`, written only by the flow's own reader (`read-library-contract.py`) into the Pack output declared exactly as `libraryContract`. Its value is `1` only after every required field validates: the 64-character hexadecimal `sourceSha256`, the literal `qualification` value `authoring-qualification`, the envelope `schema` `hima-library-insight-report/1`, a non-empty `provenance` string, and an explicit non-empty list of non-blank `unknowns`. The reading means "this bounded source contract was present and read" and nothing more: not Library API, PVT, revision, design impact, quality or customer value. There is no second number, no ratio, no derived percentage and no denominator.
8:

1: # What a pack folder holds, file by file
2: 
3: The skeleton the fabric stage compiles to. Every block below is the **smallest file of its kind that
4: this harness accepts**, with one note per field saying what that field is for. Nothing here is a
5: method: the ids, the paths, the units and the numbers are stand-ins, and what they should be for the
6: pack you are writing is the spec's to say and never this file's.
7: 
8: Read this for shape. Read the pack installed beside the folder you are authoring for a whole example
9: of the first two, written by hand for a real business. Ask `hima_pack_check` whether what you wrote
10: is a pack: it names every fault in the pack's own files, and that answer is the authority no
11: skeleton can be.
12: 
13: A pack folder holds, at its top: `contract.yml`, `graph.yml`, `semantics.yml` where the pack's own
14: readers emit value types, and the directories `rules/`, `choosers/`, `readers/`, `knowledge/` and
15: `tools/` where it has files for them. Every path in it is a plain file with a plain name — no link,
16: no hidden name, nothing but letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores in each segment.
17: 
18: ## `contract.yml` — what a Site must bind, what a generation produces, what the pack runs
19: 
20: ```yaml
21: id: example-probe            # the folder's own name; lowercase letters, digits and dashes
22: version: '1'                 # a string, and graph.yml states the same one
23: title: Example probe         # what a person reads the pack under
24: 
25: inputs:                      # what a Site binds in its own site file; the pack binds none of them
26:   - name: flowRoot
27:     description: The Golden Flow's root on the Site. Read where it lies, never written.
28:   - name: design
29:     description: What the flow is run over, spelled as the flow's own manifests spell it.
30:   - name: workspaceRoot
31:     description: Where campaign workspaces are made; the Site's permit must allow writes under it.
32: 
33: outputs:                     # what a generation leaves in its own workspace
34:   - name: measurement
35:     path: flow/out/${design}/measurement.txt   # relative to the workspace; ${…} is an input above
36:     reader: measurement-file                    # the reader that turns it into typed values
37:     description: What this generation measured. The judged file.
38:   - name: toolLog
39:     path: flow/logs/${design}/tool.log         # no reader: a file a person reads after a failure
40:     description: What the tool said while it ran.
41: 
42: environment:
43:   wrappers:                  # the first word of every command line below — a tool's argv[0] and a
44:     - make                   #   reader's; the Site's permit decides each, and a word not here is
45:     - sh                     #   refused before a campaign starts
46: 
47: workspace:
48:   copy:                      # what is copied out of flowRoot into <workspace>/flow/, once per campaign
49:     - Makefile
50:     - tools
51:     - inputs/${design}
52: 
53: tools:
54:   - id: measure
55:     file: tools/measure.sh   # the script a person can run by hand, under this folder's tools/
56:     description: One generation of the flow's own measuring stage, in the campaign's copy of it.
57:     inputs: [WORKSPACE, DESIGN, STEP_MS]   # the variables the script reads, and the only names argv may use
58:     licences:                # optional: what a job of this tool holds on the Site while it runs
59:       measuring-seat: 1      # the Site declares how many it has; a tool that holds none writes no block
60:     argv:                    # what the harness launches; argv[0] is the wrapper above
61:       - make
62:       - -C
63:       - ${WORKSPACE}/flow
64:       - DESIGN=${DESIGN}
65:       - measure
66:       - STEP_MS=${STEP_MS}
67: 
68: rules:                       # the judge rules this pack may apply, by id: this folder's rules/ first,
69:   - measurement-within-bound #   the bundle's second
70: 
71: knowledge:                   # optional: this pack's own domain knowledge, one entry per file
72:   - file: the-step-method.md
73:     purpose: why this pack changes the step the way it does
74: 
75: strategy:                    # what a run is set to for one generation; at least one knob, each whole
76:   stepMs: { type: number, unit: ms, min: 0.5, max: 10, default: 2 }
77:   shape: { type: choice, options: [plain, dense], default: plain }
78: 
79: words:                       # what a person reads each number under: one entry per goal parameter the
80:   measurement_at_most: { label: measurement at most, unit: ms }   # graph binds, one per knob above
81:   stepMs: { label: step, unit: ms }
82:   shape: { label: shape }    # a choice states no unit: a choice is measured in nothing
83: ```
84: 
85: ## Workshop declaration and graph binding
86: 
87: A Workshop is an existing `act` node variant. Its input reports are contract `outputs` produced by
88: earlier nodes; scalar `inputs` are bound by the node. Knowledge files also appear in the contract's
89: `knowledge`. The following is an additional block within `contract.yml`, not a separate file:
90: 
91: ```yaml
92: outputs:
93:   - name: measuredInput
94:     path: flow/out/${design}/measurement.txt
95:     reader: measurement-file
96:     description: The preceding tool's measurement.
97:   - name: analysis
98:     path: research/analysis/result.txt
99:     reader: measurement-file
100:     description: The script's derived measurement, checked by the reader and Judge.
101: environment:
102:   wrappers: [sh]
103: knowledge:
104:   - file: analysis-method.md
105:     purpose: How the measurements support the analysis.
106: workshops:
107:   - id: analyze
108:     purpose: Read measuredInput and write a script deriving the requested measurement from its actual data.
109:     directory: research/analysis
110:     entry: entry.sh
111:     language: sh
112:     inputs: [LIMIT]
113:     reads: [measuredInput]
114:     knowledge: [analysis-method.md]
115:     produces: analysis
116:     argv: [sh, '${ENTRY}', '${WORKSPACE}', '${LIMIT}']
117:     licences: {}             # omit when no licensed resource is needed
118: ```
119: 
120: The corresponding graph node and downstream read are real nodes, connected after the input producer:
121: 
122: ```yaml
123: - id: analyze
124:   kind: act
125:   parameters:
126:     workshop: analyze
127:     arguments:
128:       LIMIT: { from: strategy, name: stepMs }
129: - id: read-analysis
130:   kind: act
131:   parameters:
132:     observes: analysis
133: ```
134: 
135: `reads` and `produces` are exact `contract.outputs[].name` values. The model's read tool takes that
136: same output name. `@workshop-input:<name>` is an internal diagnostic label; it is not a declared
137: output, path, or read argument. `produces` names an output, not the value type its reader emits.
138: The output's reader emits types declared by `semantics.yml`; downstream Judge rules consume those
139: types. `directory` is relative to the Campaign workspace and cannot be `flow` or the readers'
140: reserved directory. `entry` is one filename. `argv[0]` is a declared Site wrapper, and `argv[1]`
141: is exactly `${ENTRY}`. A script may produce a declared output elsewhere in the Campaign workspace;
142: its code-writing tool is confined to the admitted code directory. Neither may escape the Site permit.
143: 
144: | Operand | Meaning for a controlled execution |
145: | --- | --- |
146: | `${ENTRY}` | The generated entry script inside this execution's private code directory. |
147: | `${WORKSPACE}` | The Campaign root containing `flow/` and the declared output paths. |
148: | `${WORKSHOP}` | This execution's private code directory beneath the declared `directory`, including its execution identity. |
149: 
150: This example passes `WORKSPACE`, so shell `$1` is the Campaign root and `$2` is LIMIT. Its input
151: and output paths start from `$1`. A script needing helper files in its private code directory may
152: also need a `WORKSHOP` operand; use the approved spec's exact operand order and document each shell
153: position. Obtain the Campaign root from `WORKSPACE`, never by assuming a number of parent directories
154: above `WORKSHOP`. The example supplies file shape, not permission to replace the spec's argv.
155: 
156: Reader scripts have their own argv: below `$1` is `${REPORT}` and `$2` is `${OUT}`. These are argv
157: arrays; shell commands, pipes and redirections belong inside scripts.
158: 
159: ## `graph.yml` — the four node kinds, the outcomes the edges are taken on, and the one edge back
160: 
161: The block illustrates node and edge syntax. For an executable Explore method, supply the actual
162: constraint and Goal rules from the spec: the preceding Judge needs at least two ordered rules,
163: constraint first and Goal second. The single rule skeleton here does not supply that whole method.
164: 
165: ```yaml
166: id: example-probe            # the contract's id
167: version: '1'                 # the contract's version
168: entry: measure               # the node a campaign starts at
169: 
170: nodes:
171:   - id: measure              # act: run one of the contract's tools on the Site and wait for it
172:     kind: act
173:     parameters:
174:       tool: measure
175:       arguments:             # what the Run supplies for this generation
176:         STEP_MS: { from: strategy, name: stepMs }
177: 
178:   - id: read-measurement     # act: read one of the contract's outputs into the ledger
179:     kind: act
180:     parameters:
181:       observes: measurement
182: 
183:   - id: judge                # judge: apply rules in order; the edge out is chosen by the first one's outcome
184:     kind: judge
185:     parameters:
186:       rules: [measurement-within-bound]
187:       bind:                  # what binds each parameter a rule declares
188:         bound_ms: { from: goal, name: measurement_at_most }
189: 
190:   - id: next-step            # explore: choose the next strategy, or open a loop of its own
191:     kind: explore
192:     parameters:
193:       chooser: step-back-off # by id, exactly as a rule is named
194:       bind:                  # the numbers the chooser leaves to the pack author
195:         marginMs: 0.05
196:       converge:              # optional, and all four together: when this loop has stopped learning
197:         read: measured       # one of the chooser's own `reads`
198:         band: 0.05           # how far apart two generations must be to count as movement
199:         generations: 1       # how many successive generations must have moved by less than that
200:         generationLimit: 6   # what this pack thinks a campaign of it should be allowed at most
201: 
202:   - id: blocked              # wait: where a run stops for a person once its retries are spent
203:     kind: wait
204:     parameters:
205:       blocker: hard-blocker
206: 
207: edges:
208:   - { from: measure, to: read-measurement }            # an act node's one unlabelled edge out
209:   - { from: read-measurement, to: judge }
210:   - { from: judge, to: next-step, outcome: PASS }      # a judge node's edges carry their outcome
211:   - { from: judge, to: next-step, outcome: FAIL }
212:   - { from: next-step, to: measure, revisit: true }    # the loop: the only edge that goes back
213: ```
214: 
215: Read actual edges to audit endings. Judge routing uses the first rule's outcome, while an Explore
216: owner decision uses the current required Judge evidence. A goal-met decision ends the Run before a
217: revisit; a next-strategy decision follows the revisit only if the original generation budget allows
218: it. A terminal Judge PASS alone supplies no Campaign goal-met decision. Waits remain legitimate
219: where the approved spec calls for human clearance; compare each actual outcome path with that spec.
220: Comments such as "PASS is terminal" cannot override a PASS edge whose destination is a wait node.
221: 
222: ## `semantics.yml` — what the value types this pack's own readers emit mean
223: 
224: Written **only** where this pack's own readers emit a value type. A pack whose outputs are all read
225: by readers the harness ships declares none and writes no such file.
226: 
227: The two qualifier vocabularies are the harness's own and are **fixed**: `mode` is `setup` or `hold`,
228: `scope` is `all` or `reg2reg`. Declaring either means every reading of that type carries one of the
229: listed words; declaring neither means a reading of it carries no qualifier at all.
230: 
231: ```yaml
232: values:
233:   measured_ms:               # the slug a reader emits and a rule or chooser reads
234:     unit: ms                 # what a value of it is measured in; every reading is held to this
235:     mode: [setup, hold]      # optional: the analysis passes a value of it can belong to
236:     scope: [all, reg2reg]    # optional: the path groups a value of it can cover
237:     description: what this generation measured, as the file states it
238: ```
239: 
240: ## `rules/<id>.yml` — one judge rule
241: 
242: ```yaml
243: id: measurement-within-bound # the file's own name, without the .yml
244: version: '1'
245: title: The measurement is within the bound the run was started with
246: parameter:                   # optional: the one value a node binds at judge time
247:   name: bound_ms
248:   unit: ms
249: requires:                    # what must have been observed for this rule to have an opinion at all
250:   - type: measured_ms
251: subject:                     # the value the predicate is about
252:   type: measured_ms
253: predicate:
254:   op: lte                    # lte, gte and the like
255:   threshold: { parameter: bound_ms }   # or a number written here
256:   unit: ms
257: ```
258: 
259: ## `choosers/<id>.yml` — one explore move, as data
260: 
261: ```yaml
262: id: step-back-off
263: version: '1'
264: title: Take the step back by what the last generation missed by
265: parameter:                   # the one number the pack binds in its explore node's `bind:`
266:   name: marginMs
267:   unit: ms
268: reads:                       # what is read out of the run's latest observation, by type
269:   measured: { type: measured_ms, unit: ms }
270: decide:                      # first matching clause wins
271:   - when: { constraint: PASS, goal: PASS }
272:     goalMet: true            # the goal is reached; there is no next strategy
273:   - when: { constraint: PASS }
274:     next:                    # sets this pack's own strategy knobs by name; a knob not named carries over
275:       stepMs: { sum: [measured, marginMs] }
276:   - when: { constraint: FAIL }
277:     next:
278:       stepMs: { sum: [measured, { neg: marginMs }] }
279: ```
280: 
281: ## `readers/<id>.yml` and its script under `tools/` — a reader of this pack's own
282: 
283: ```yaml
284: id: measurement-file
285: version: '1'
286: file: tools/read-measurement.sh   # under this folder's tools/, and a plain file
287: argv:                             # every word is a literal, or exactly one of the four placeholders
288:   - sh                            # argv[0] is the wrapper: a literal word the contract declares
289:   - ${READER}                     # the script's path on the Site
290:   - ${REPORT}                     # the output the contract pointed it at
291:   - ${OUT}                        # the file the script must write
292: reportKind: example-measurement   # a word for the record; never sniffed
293: emits: [measured_ms]              # every value type it writes, each declared in the semantics
294: ```
295: 
296: Its script, under this folder's `tools/`, launched by the harness as a job under the Site's permit
297: with the report and the output file as arguments:
298: 
299: ```sh
300: #!/bin/sh
301: # tools/read-measurement.sh — reads $1 (the report) and writes the reading document to $2.
302: set -eu
303: printf '{"values":[{"type":"measured_ms","unit":"ms","mode":"setup","scope":"all","value":%s}]}\n' \
304:   "$(awk '/^measured/ { print $2 }' "$1")" > "$2"
305: ```
306: 
307: What it writes to `${OUT}` — one JSON document, and exit 0:
308: 
309: ```json
310: { "values": [ { "type": "measured_ms", "unit": "ms", "mode": "setup", "scope": "all", "value": 2.5 } ] }
311: ```
312: 
313: A value carries `mode` and `scope` exactly when the semantics above declare them for its type, and
314: the word it carries is one of the declared ones. It may also carry `group` (the tool's own name for
315: the path group the number came from) and, where the report did not state the number at all,
316: `"value": null` with `unknownReason` saying why — never a zero standing in for a number nobody read.
317: A value whose type, unit or qualifiers are not the declared ones is refused, and the reading never
318: becomes an observation.
319: 
320: ## `knowledge/<file>.md` — one piece of this pack's domain knowledge
321: 
322: A plain Markdown file, one per entry of the contract's `knowledge:`, written for the purpose that
323: entry gives it. It guides the executing Agent; it does not establish measured facts. Explain the
324: method symbolically. Include a worked numeric result only with the exact input and parameters and
325: an observed calculation or checked result that produced it; otherwise leave the result unverified.
326: An example value copied from another dataset cannot serve as this dataset's expected answer.
327: 
328: ```markdown
329: # Why this pack changes the step the way it does
330: 
331: <the reasoning, in the author's own words, for the purpose the contract declares>
332: ```
333: 
334: ## The five records the pipeline writes
335: 
336: Each is written by one stage, and each is what carries the folder one rung further up. They are the
337: authoring account and not the pack — no campaign reads one — and the digest of the files a campaign
338: runs is taken without them.
339: 
340: | File | Written by | Sections, in this order |
341: | --- | --- | --- |
342: | `INTENT.md` | `/hima-grill` | `Business`, `Golden Flow`, `Answers`, `Ambiguities resolved`, `Knowledge applied` |
343: | `SPEC.md` | `/hima-spec` | `Goal template`, `Constraints`, `Run contract`, `Semantics`, `Judge rules`, `Choosers`, `Endings`, `Workshops`, `Knowledge` |
344: | `FABRIC.md` | `/hima-fabric` | `Files written`, `Gaps`, `Reviews` |
345: | `TEST.md` | `/hima-test` | `Site`, `Run`, `Ending`, `Generations`, `Code`, `Refusals`, `Disagreements` |
346: | `VERSION.yml` | `/hima-release`, through the harness's own verb | `pack`, `version`, `released`, `test: { record, run }`, `files:` — one sha256 per file |
347: 
348: A record validates when its ordered `##` headings are **exactly** those sections: nothing missing,
349: nothing extra, nothing twice, nothing out of order, nothing empty. `VERSION.yml` is the one of the
350: five nobody writes by hand: every hash in it is computed by the harness over the bytes in the folder.

(End of file - total 350 lines)
</content>

1: # The run contract of the opene902 timing probe: what a Site must bind before this pack can run,
2: # what a generation produces inside the Campaign workspace, and what the pack runs on the Site.
3: # `/hima pack check <pack> --site <site>` reads this file against a Site's own and reports every
4: # input that is not bound, every wrapper the Permit will not run, and every rule or reader that does
5: # not exist.
6: id: opene902-timing-probe
7: version: '2'
8: title: opene902 timing probe
9: 
10: # What a Site binds, in its site file under `bindings:`. The same pack runs on another Site by
11: # editing that file, never this one.
12: inputs:
13:   - name: flowRoot
14:     description: >-
15:       The Golden Flow's root on the Site: the directory holding the makefile the flow is driven by.
16:       Read-only to a Campaign — a generation runs in its own copy of it, never here.
17:   - name: design
18:     description: The design the flow builds, spelled as the flow's own manifests spell it.
19:   - name: workspaceRoot
20:     description: >-
21:       Where Campaign workspaces are created. The Site's Permit must allow writes under it; nothing
22:       the pack does writes anywhere else.
23: 
24: # What a generation leaves in its Campaign workspace. Paths are relative to the workspace, with
25: # `${design}` bound from the Site's binding of that input.
26: outputs:
27:   - name: qorReport
28:     path: flow/results/${design}/syn/report/qor.rpt
29:     reader: dc-qor-report
30:     description: The Design Compiler qor report of the generation just synthesized. The judged report.
31:   - name: synthesisLog
32:     path: flow/logs/${design}/dc_shell.log
33:     description: What dc_shell said while it ran. Read by a person after a failure, not by a reader.
34: 
35: # What the Site must let this pack run: the first word of every tool's command line. The Permit's
36: # `allowedWrappers` decides each one, so a pack cannot introduce a command a Site owner never allowed.
37: environment:
38:   wrappers:
39:     - make
40: 
41: # How a Campaign workspace is prepared from the bound flow root, once per Campaign. The copy lands in
42: # `<workspace>/flow/`, which is the pack anatomy's fixed place for it (see README, "Pack anatomy").
43: workspace:
44:   copy:
45:     - Makefile
46:     - flows
47:     - manifests
48:     - tools
49:     - build/${design}
50:     - sources/${design}
51: 
52: # The pack's tools. Each names the file a person reads and runs by hand, and the command line the
53: # fabric launches on the Site. `${NAME}` in `argv` is one of the tool's declared `inputs`, which are
54: # the environment variables the tool's own script reads.
55: tools:
56:   - id: synth
57:     file: tools/synth.sh
58:     description: >-

1: # The opene902 timing probe as a HimaFabric graph, and the Loop it explores in: synthesize at the
2: # strategy's clock period, read what it produced, judge it, choose the next strategy — and go round
3: # again with that strategy, generation after generation, until the goal is met, the periods stop
4: # moving, or the campaign's generation limit is spent.
5: #
6: # Four node kinds and no more (CONTEXT.md): act, judge, explore, wait. An act node has one unlabelled
7: # edge out; a judge node's edges carry the outcome they are taken on. A node with no outgoing edge
8: # ends the Run.
9: #
10: # The loop is the last edge below, `next-period` back to `synthesize`, marked `revisit: true` (D43).
11: # Following it is what opens the next generation, with the period the explore node just chose. It is
12: # the only edge in this graph that goes backwards, and the only kind of edge allowed to: a loop a
13: # reader cannot see in this file is a loop the engine would be running behind it.
14: id: opene902-timing-probe
15: version: '2'
16: entry: synthesize
17: 
18: nodes:
19:   # Act: run the pack's tool on the Site, in the Campaign workspace, and wait for it.
20:   - id: synthesize
21:     kind: act
22:     parameters:
23:       tool: synth
24:       # Only the strategy knob is chosen per generation. WORKSPACE, FLOW_ROOT, DESIGN and CAMPAIGN
25:       # are the Run's own workspace and the Site's bindings, which the fabric already holds — and
26:       # which a node may not bind: a pack that named one here would not load.
27:       arguments:
28:         PERIOD_NS: { from: strategy, name: periodNs }
29: 
30:   # Act: read the report that generation produced into HimaLedger, through the contract's own reader.
31:   - id: read-qor
32:     kind: act
33:     parameters:
34:       observes: qorReport
35: 
36:   # Judge: the setup rule first, then the goal rule whose target the Run's goal binds. The outgoing
37:   # edge is chosen by the outcome of the first rule listed.
38:   - id: judge
39:     kind: judge
40:     parameters:
41:       rules:
42:         - setup-wns-all-nonnegative
43:         - clock-period-at-most
44:       bind:
45:         target_period_ns: { from: goal, name: target_period_ns }
46: 
47:   # Method version 2: a met constraint is tested one step tighter; a violation proposes
48:   # period + |slack| - stepNs. This candidate is a hypothesis, not a measured closed period.
49:   # Convergence means the observed periods stopped moving, even if setup still fails.
50:   # Only a generation passing both setup and goal can end goal-met.
51:   # generationLimit is a budget bound, not a claim that the goal is reachable.
52:   - id: next-period
53:     kind: explore
54:     parameters:
55:       chooser: over-constraining-push
56:       bind:
57:         stepNs: 0.05
58:       converge:
59:         read: period
60:         band: 0.05
61:         generations: 1
62:         generationLimit: 6
63: 
64:   # Wait: where a Run stops for a person once its Retry allowance is spent. Nothing draws an edge
65:   # here, and nothing needs to: a Hard blocker is routed to the graph's wait node by the fabric
66:   # itself, exactly as an UNDETERMINED the pack labelled no edge for is. A pack declares where its
67:   # Runs wait; it does not have to draw an edge from every node that might fail.
68:   - id: blocked
69:     kind: wait
70:     parameters:
71:       blocker: hard-blocker
72: 
73: edges:
74:   - { from: synthesize, to: read-qor }
75:   - { from: read-qor, to: judge }
76:   - { from: judge, to: next-period, outcome: PASS }
77:   - { from: judge, to: next-period, outcome: FAIL }
78:   # The loop: taken only when the decision chose a next strategy. A decision of goal met or converged
79:   # has no edge to take, and the Run ends where it stands.
80:   - { from: next-period, to: synthesize, revisit: true }

<content>
1: # opene902 timing probe
2: 
3: A HimaPack that answers one question about one design: **which tested clock periods satisfy setup timing, and what should be tried next?** It synthesizes `opene902` at a chosen period in a workspace of its
4: own, reads the qor report the run produced, judges it against the setup constraint and the goal, and
5: chooses the next period to try from what it measured — never from what it hoped. Then it goes round
6: again with that period, and keeps going until the goal is met, the periods stop moving, or the
7: Campaign's generation allowance is spent.
8: 
9: This is the first pack, and it is deliberately the smallest thing that is still a real Campaign: one
10: strategy knob, one tool, one report, two rules, one chooser, one loop. Everything a bigger pack will
11: need — more knobs, more reports, a drill-down loop inside this one — is the same parts with more in
12: each.
13: 
14: Method version **2** changes only the default chooser binding from the legacy `timing-push`
15: guard band to the existing `over-constraining-push` step. Graph and contract both declare version 2.
16: The reference graph topology, tools, reader and Judge rules remain unchanged.
17: 
18: ## What one generation does
19: 
20: 1. **`synthesize`** (act) runs `tools/synth.sh` on the Site: `make … synth` inside the Campaign's own
21:    copy of the flow, at the strategy's clock period, forced so no generation reuses another's
22:    netlist.
23: 2. **`read-qor`** (act) reads `flow/results/<design>/syn/report/qor.rpt` through the
24:    `dc-qor-report@1` reader, which turns it into typed values: setup WNS, setup TNS, the clock
25:    period the run actually used, hold WNS, and cell area.
26: 3. **`judge`** (judge) applies two rules to those values and writes a verdict for each.
27: 4. **`next-period`** (explore) runs the `over-constraining-push` chooser over the verdicts and the values and
28:    records the next strategy with its reasoning.
29: 
30: Then, if the decision was a next period, the Run follows the `revisit` edge from `next-period` back
31: to `synthesize` and does all four again as the next generation, at that period. A `blocked` wait node
32: is declared for the Hard blockers a node's spent Retry allowance produces; nothing draws an edge to
33: it, because the fabric routes a Run there itself.
34: 
35: ## The Campaign: generation after generation
36: 
37: A **generation** is one pass of those four nodes: one synthesis at one period, read, judged, decided.
38: The first is generation one, and every record it leaves — the node transitions, the Job, the
39: observation, the verdicts, the decision — says which generation it belongs to, so the ledger reads as
40: the exploration ran. The Retry allowance is per node *per generation*: a synthesis that failed twice
41: in generation two starts generation three's allowance afresh, because a retry under a new period is
42: not a third go at the old one.
43: 
44: A Campaign of this pack ends in one of four ways, and the run row says which:
45: 
46: - **`ended-goal-met`** — a generation closed its setup timing *and* reached the target period. The
47:   question is answered and no further licence-minute is spent on it.
48: - **`ended-converged`** — the exploration has stopped learning. `next-period` declares what that
49:   means, as data, in the chooser's own vocabulary:
50: 
51:   ```yaml
52:   converge:
53:     read: period        # one of the chooser's own reads
54:     band: 0.05          # ns: how far apart two generations' periods must be to count as movement
55:     generations: 1      # how many successive generations must have moved by less than that
56:     generationLimit: 6  # this pack's default allowance, which a person may override
57:   ```
58: 
59:   The 0.05 ns band is the exploration step. This ending states only that consecutive
60:   measured periods moved by less than that band. It does **not** prove the Goal was met,
61:   the last generation met setup, or a global optimum was found. A repeated violation may
62:   converge; use the recorded verdicts to distinguish it from a measured closed result.
63: 
64:   The decision record carries the whole rule — the read, the band, the generations counted, and the
65:   periods compared — so a person can re-derive the ending from one record, and `/hima status` and the
66:   workbench card say it in words.
67: - **`ended-budget-exhausted`** — a meter ran out. `generation-limit` is the Loop's own: the Campaign
68:   reached the generation it was allowed and the revisit that would have opened the next one did not
69:   happen, with the period it would have tried still on record. `time-box` is the other.
70: - **`waiting`** — a node spent its Retry allowance and the Run is at `blocked`, for a person.
71: 
72: The generation limit is a **Budget** meter and not a convergence: convergence is what the exploration
73: learned, the limit is what the Campaign was allowed to spend learning it. `converge.generationLimit`
74: above is this pack's default; `/hima run … --generations <n>` (and the same field on the start route)
75: overrides it, and what the Run is actually held to is on its Budget from the moment it opens.
76: 
77: The local Site generates **stand-in** reports, with `setup_wns = min(0, period − 2.20)` ns.
78: These are controlled test numbers, not measured Design Compiler or silicon improvements.
79: From 2.30 ns, method 2 gives the following bounded examples:
80: 
81: | Goal | Measured periods (ns) | Ending |
82: | --- | --- | --- |
83: | 2.25 ns | 2.30, 2.25 | goal met; the last generation passes both rules |
84: | 2.00 ns | 2.30, 2.25, 2.20, 2.15, 2.15 | converged; the last two generations violate setup and the Goal remains unmet |
85: | 2.00 ns, one generation allowed, starting at 2.00 | 2.00 | generation limit; no measured setup-PASS result exists |
86: 
87: For the converged example, the best **measured setup-PASS** period is 2.20 ns. The 2.15 ns
88: requested period is a violation, and `period + |slack|` is a hypothesis about a possible period,
89: not a new measurement. An unexecuted next Strategy must never be included among measured results.
90: If there is no completed setup-PASS observation, there is no measured closed result to report.
91: The report's generation rows, verdicts, observation IDs and raw qor/logs provide the evidence;
92: this Pack does not add a second best-result computation to the Harness.
93: 
94: ## The goal template
95: 
96: A Campaign binds one number when it starts:
97: 
98: ```
99: target_period_ns = <the clock period this design must close on, in ns>
100: ```
101: 
102: That number is bound into the goal rule `clock-period-at-most@1`, whose predicate is
103: `clock_period ≤ target_period_ns`. The rule file states the comparison; the Campaign states the
104: target. One rule therefore serves every target period, and the run cannot widen its own goal to
105: manufacture a pass — the bound value lands on the verdict, where a person can read what was actually
106: asked for.
107: 
108: `target_period_ns` is the name the harness carries it under; what a person reads is the words this
109: pack declares for it under `words:` in `contract.yml` — **clock period at most**, in **ns**. So a
110: card and `/hima status` say `goal: clock period at most 2.3 ns`, not `goal: target_period_ns=2.3`,
111: while every route still answers under the name. The number keeps whatever precision it was given: a
112: face shows what the ledger holds and rounds nothing. A pack that declares no words for a number shows
113: it under the name; this one declares both of its numbers, this and the strategy knob below.
114: 
115: The setup constraint is the same one step 1 checks, unparameterised:
116: `setup-wns-all-nonnegative@1`, `setup_wns ≥ 0` over all paths. A generation that closes its own
117: setup timing but misses the target is a real result, not a failure: it says the design closes, but
118: not yet where the goal is.
119: 
120: The judge applies the rules in the order `graph.yml` lists them, and the outgoing edge is chosen by
121: the outcome of the **first** — the setup rule. The goal rule decides whether the Campaign is done,
122: not which way the graph goes.
123: 
124: ## The strategy knob
125: 
126: One knob: **`periodNs`**, the clock period handed to `CLOCK_PERIOD_NS` for that generation. It is
127: the only thing that changes between generations of this pack. The flow accepts it as a command-line
128: variable, so nothing in the flow is edited to try a new value.
129: 
130: The knob is this pack's, declared in `contract.yml` under `strategy:` with everything about it in
131: one place — its type, its unit, its bounds and the value a campaign starts at:
132: 
133: ```yaml
134: strategy:
135:   periodNs: { type: number, unit: ns, min: 0.5, max: 10, default: 2.30 }
136: ```
137: 
138: The bounds are what a person could plausibly ask *this flow* for and not what this design closes at:
139: they hold every period this pack has been run at on the stand-in and on the reference site, and they
140: refuse a mistyped `0` or `100` before a campaign exists, in the same words at the window's start
141: form, at `--set periodNs=<ns>` and in a request body. The default is what the start form fills in
142: and what a run that sets nothing is started at.
143: 
144: Its words, declared beside the goal parameter's under `words:`, are **clock period** in **ns**: a
145: face says `strategy: clock period 2.25 ns`, and the run row and the routes go on carrying
146: `periodNs`.
147: 
148: The period a generation was judged on is read back from the report (`clock_period`), never assumed
149: from the number that was asked for. A tool that silently clamped the period, or a reused netlist from
150: an earlier run, would otherwise be judged as if it had honoured the request.
151: 
152: ## The chooser and its exploration step
153: 
154: `over-constraining-push` uses **stepNs = 0.05 ns**. Given the recorded setup verdict,
155: goal verdict, `clock_period` and `setup_wns`:
156: 
157: - **Both PASS**: end goal-met; do not propose another experiment.
158: - **Setup PASS, Goal not met**: try `clock_period − stepNs`. A met constraint does not
159:   need to expose positive slack for exploration to continue.
160: - **Setup FAIL**: try `clock_period + |setup_wns| − stepNs`. This is a proposed experiment,
161:   not evidence that the design closes at the inferred period.
162: 
163: Goal-met is checked first, then the Pack's convergence rule, then a next Strategy.
164: The chooser remains deterministic YAML in `choosers/over-constraining-push.yml`;
165: no model participates in this sample's strategy selection. The Ledger decision records its
166: inputs, parameters and cited verdicts/observation. Broader AI research belongs to the later Pack.
167: 
168: ### Why the default changed
169: 
170: The historical Step 3 reference-site trace reported zero setup slack at met constraints.
171: The old `timing-push` PASS clause therefore increased the requested period by 0.05 ns every
172: generation. On the calibrated stand-in, starting at 2.30 ns produces 2.30, 2.35, 2.40,
173: 2.45, 2.50, 2.55 and stops at the generation limit. That failure remains an explicitly
174: named `legacy-timing-push-probe` test variant; the old chooser file is retained unchanged.
175: 
176: Version 2 avoids relying on positive margin in that case. The local examples prove the
177: mechanism under their stated arithmetic, not a universal property of Design Compiler, all
178: designs or synthesis settings. Real Site efficacy requires a separate measured validation.
179: Historical records belong to their original method version and must not be relabeled as v2.
180: 
181: ## What a Site must bind
182: 
183: `contract.yml` names three inputs; a Site binds them in its own file under `bindings:`.
184: 
185: | Input | On `linglong` | On the local site |
186: | --- | --- | --- |
187: | `flowRoot` | `/data/eda/project/design_zoo` — the Site's Design Zoo | the generated stand-in flow |
188: | `design` | `opene902` | `opene902` |
189: | `workspaceRoot` | `/data/eda/project/hima_harness` | the isolated home's workspace |
190: 
191: Nothing else about the pack changes between the two. That is what the run contract is for:
192: `/hima pack check opene902-timing-probe --site <site>` says, before anything runs, whether a Site can
193: host this pack — every input bound, every tool's first word a wrapper the Permit allows, every rule
194: and reader resolvable, and every licence a tool holds declared by the Site in at least that number.
195: 
196: ## What a generation holds
197: 
198: `synth` holds **one `Design-Compiler` seat** for as long as its Job runs, declared on the tool in
199: `contract.yml`. A Site says how many seats it has under `capacity.licences` — `linglong` declares 99
200: — and the count is held across every Run of that Site, exactly as the parallel job cap is, because a
201: licence belongs to the Site and not to a Campaign. A launch that would take one seat too many waits
202: for one to come free, and says so on the node; a Site that declares fewer seats than this tool holds
203: (or none, which is what a node-locked tool's `0` means) cannot host the pack at all, and the check
204: says so rather than letting a Run wait for a seat that will never come free.
205: 
206: The other tool a person might expect here — Innovus — is not in this pack, which is why nothing
207: declares the reference site's `Innovus_Impl_System: 0`.
208: 
209: ## Where a generation runs
210: 
211: Never in `flowRoot`. `/hima pack prepare` copies the flow's makefile, its `flows/` and `manifests/`
212: directories, and the design's `build/` and `sources/` trees (about 56 MB for `opene902`) into
213: `<workspaceRoot>/<campaign>/flow/`, and every generation of that Campaign runs there. The flow
214: derives its project root from its own location, so the copy builds into the copy.
215: 
216: The one thing that does *not* follow from the copy's location is the container the flow's wrapper
217: runs in: it creates a container by name and binds the project root into it, so a copy run under the
218: Site's own container name would write the Site's own results after all. Hence
219: `EDA_CONTAINER_NAME=hima-<campaign>` on every tool line, and the container's name recorded in the
220: workspace's `workspace.json` so a later cleanup knows what to remove.
221: 
222: ## What the Campaign leaves for the next one
223: 
224: Every ended Run of this pack writes its own technical report into the Campaign workspace, beside the
225: results: `<workspaceRoot>/<campaign>/hima-experience/<runId>.md` for the people who read it and
226: `<runId>.json` for the programs that do. Nothing in this pack's three files asks for it — the harness
227: writes it for every pack, whatever ending the Run reached, a cancel and a spent time box included —
228: and it is written where the results are and left there, because the evidence of a Campaign belongs to
229: the Site owner and outlives the session that produced it. HimaLedger keeps only each file's path,
230: size and SHA-256, so a person who fetches one months later can hold it against what the Campaign
231: actually wrote.
232: 
233: What the Markdown holds is this pack's own story: the ending and why, the goal that was bound and
234: the Site it ran on, every Budget meter against its bound, one row per generation with the period it
235: asked for, the period and slack it measured, its verdicts and its decision, then a paragraph per
236: generation saying the same in sentences — *It asked the flow for 2.25 ns and measured 2.25 ns, with
237: 0.00 ns of setup slack. HimaJudge found PASS on setup-wns-all-nonnegative, FAIL on
238: clock-period-at-most. The decision was …* — and finally the path the Run took, any Hard blockers,
239: and any cancel. So the file answers, without the ledger, the two questions a pack author is asked
240: about a Campaign that has finished: what did it learn, and why did it stop.
241: 
242: A person reads it in three places without going to the Site: the card's evidence drawer on an ended
243: Run, the `.md` route the drawer links to, and `/hima status <run>`, which names both paths.

(End of file - total 243 lines)
</content>

5: # candidate count or an adoption ratio declares it where the method lives (D46). What is here is what
6: # every pack of this kind would otherwise write out again — the base timing quantities the bundled

11: # The four slack types are the ones that carry both, because a slack is a statement about one

13: #

1: # The goal rule: the run's clock period may be at most the caller's bound target. `parameter`
2: # declares the one value a caller binds at judge time (`--param target_period_ns=<ns>`); the
3: # predicate's `threshold: { parameter: ... }` takes its place instead of a number fixed in this file.
4: id: clock-period-at-most
5: version: '1'
6: title: Clock period is at most the bound target period
7: parameter:
8:   name: target_period_ns

1: # The chooser of the opene902 timing probe, and of any pack whose knob is a clock period judged
2: # against a setup constraint. Data, never code (D38): a person adjusts the push rule here, beside
3: # the judge rules, without reading TypeScript.
4: #
5: # - The constraint PASSED — the design closed with slack to spare. Push: the next period is the
6: #   period the report stated, minus that slack, plus the guard band. Taking the whole slack back
7: #   would land exactly on the edge the tool just reported, which is where estimation error lives.
8: # - The constraint FAILED — the design missed by the slack it reported. Back off by exactly that
9: #   much, plus the guard band.
10: # - Both the constraint and the goal PASSED — the design closed and reached what the Run was for.
11: #   There is no next strategy; the decision is that the Goal is met.
12: id: timing-push
13: version: '1'
14: title: Push the clock period against the measured setup margin
15: 
16: # The one number a pack binds, in its explore node's `bind:`. What the chooser leaves on the table on
17: # purpose is the pack author's judgement, not this file's.
18: parameter:
19:   name: guardBandNs
20:   unit: ns
21: 
22: # What is read out of the Run's latest observation. The period is read from the report, never from
23: # the number the Run asked for: a tool that clamped the period, or a netlist reused from an earlier
24: # generation, would otherwise be pushed against as if it had honoured the request.
25: reads:
26:   period: { type: clock_period, unit: ns }
27:   slack: { type: setup_wns, unit: ns }
28: 
29: # First matching `when` wins. `constraint` is the verdict of the judge node's first rule — the one
30: # the outgoing edge was chosen by — and `goal` the verdict of its goal rule. A generation no clause
31: # matches is answered with a reason, never with a period computed from a substituted zero.
32: # `next` sets the pack's own strategy knobs by name, and a knob it does not name carries over. This
33: # chooser is for a pack whose knob is a clock period; the name below is the one such a contract
34: # declares it under, and `/hima pack check` holds the two against each other before a campaign runs.
35: decide:
36:   - when: { constraint: PASS, goal: PASS }
37:     goalMet: true
38:   - when: { constraint: PASS }
39:     next:
40:       periodNs: { sum: [period, { neg: slack }, guardBandNs] }
41:   - when: { constraint: FAIL }
42:     next:
43:       periodNs: { sum: [period, { abs: slack }, guardBandNs] }

(End of file - total 43 lines)
</content>

<content>
1: # The chooser of a timing push that knows its business: it over-constrains on purpose and reads the
2: # violation the tool answers with. Data, never code (D38), beside `timing-push.yml`, for a pack whose
3: # knob is a clock period judged against a setup constraint.
4: #
5: # Why a second push rule exists at all (D45). `timing-push` asks a met period how much margin it had
6: # and pushes by the answer. A tool that reports no margin for a met period does not answer that
7: # question: it states a setup slack of exactly 0.00 whenever the period it was given is met, because
8: # it stops optimizing the moment the constraint is satisfied. So on such a tool that clause reads
9: # `period − 0 + guardBand` and loosens the period by the guard band every generation, which is the
10: # trace the step-3 acceptance on the reference site recorded (D45) — six generations walking from
11: # 2.28 ns out to 2.53 ns, converging on nothing.
12: #
13: # The method here never asks a met period what it had to spare. It asks for less than it believes is
14: # possible and lets the tool say by how much it was wrong:
15: #
16: # - The constraint PASSED — the tool said nothing about the margin, because a met period is all it
17: #   says. Take one step tighter and ask again; that is the over-constraining, and `stepNs` is how
18: #   coarse the walk in is.
19: # - The constraint FAILED — now the tool has stated something: the design missed by `|slack|`, so
20: #   `period + |slack|` is the period it can actually close at. Ask for one step less than that. The
21: #   next generation misses by that same step, states the same achievable period, and asks for the
22: #   same number again — two successive generations asking and measuring the same period, which is
23: #   what a pack's `converge:` calls having stopped learning. The violation is on record, which is
24: #   the fact the Campaign was run to find.
25: # - Both the constraint and the goal PASSED — the design closed and reached what the Run was for.
26: #   There is no next strategy; the decision is that the Goal is met.
27: #
28: # So a Campaign on this chooser ends `ended-goal-met` when the goal is reachable and
29: # `ended-converged` one step below the achievable period when it is not, on a tool that reports zero
30: # slack for a met period and on one that reports a real margin alike: the PASS clause never reads the
31: # margin, so it cannot be misled by a tool that has none to give.
32: id: over-constraining-push
33: version: '1'
34: title: Over-constrain the clock period by one step and read the violation
35: 
36: # The one number a pack binds, in its explore node's `bind:`: how far the walk in moves each
37: # generation while nothing is violated, and how far above the violated period the exploration settles.
38: parameter:
39:   name: stepNs
40:   unit: ns
41: 
42: # What is read out of the Run's latest observation, exactly as `timing-push` reads it: the period is
43: # the one the report stated and never the one the Run asked for, so a tool that clamped the period is
44: # not pushed against as if it had honoured the request.
45: reads:
46:   period: { type: clock_period, unit: ns }
47:   slack: { type: setup_wns, unit: ns }
48: 
49: # First matching `when` wins. `constraint` is the verdict of the judge node's first rule — the one
50: # the outgoing edge was chosen by — and `goal` the verdict of its goal rule.
51: # `next` sets the pack's own strategy knobs by name, and a knob it does not name carries over. This
52: # chooser is for a pack whose knob is a clock period; the name below is the one such a contract
53: # declares it under, and `/hima pack check` holds the two against each other before a campaign runs.
54: decide:
55:   - when: { constraint: PASS, goal: PASS }
56:     goalMet: true
57:   - when: { constraint: PASS }
58:     next:
59:       periodNs: { sum: [period, { neg: stepNs }] }
60:   - when: { constraint: FAIL }
61:     next:
62:       periodNs: { sum: [period, { abs: slack }, { neg: stepNs }] }

1: #!/bin/sh
2: # The `synth` tool of the opene902 timing probe: one synthesis generation at a chosen clock period.
3: #
4: # The command line below is the one `contract.yml` declares for this tool, so a person can reproduce
5: # a generation by hand exactly as HimaFabric runs it:
6: #
7: #   WORKSPACE=/data/eda/project/hima_harness/<campaign> \
8: #   FLOW_ROOT=/data/eda/project/design_zoo \
9: #   DESIGN=opene902 PERIOD_NS=2.20 CAMPAIGN=<campaign> \
10: #   sh packs/opene902-timing-probe/tools/synth.sh
11: #
12: # Three things about that line are the whole point of it:
13: #   - `-C "$WORKSPACE/flow"` runs the Campaign's own copy of the flow. The flow derives its project
14: #     root from its own location, so the copy builds into the copy and the Site's own results under
15: #     $FLOW_ROOT are never written.
16: #   - `FORCE_SYNTH=1` because the flow reuses an existing netlist otherwise, and a generation that
17: #     reused the previous one's netlist would be judged on a period it never ran at.
18: #   - `EDA_CONTAINER_NAME=hima-$CAMPAIGN` because the flow's wrapper CREATES a container of that name
19: #     on first use and binds $PROJECT_ROOT into it. Running the copy under the Site's own container
20: #     name would bind the Site's flow instead and write the Site's results (D19).
21: set -eu
22: 
23: : "${WORKSPACE:?the Campaign workspace on the Site}"
24: : "${FLOW_ROOT:?the Site's flow root, for the record: the generation runs in the workspace copy}"
25: : "${DESIGN:?the design to synthesize}"
26: : "${PERIOD_NS:?the clock period this generation is the strategy for}"
27: : "${CAMPAIGN:?the Campaign this generation belongs to, which names its container}"
28: 
29: exec make -C "$WORKSPACE/flow" DESIGN="$DESIGN" synth CLOCK_PERIOD_NS="$PERIOD_NS" FORCE_SYNTH=1 EDA_CONTAINER_NAME="hima-$CAMPAIGN"

</content>

1: # The run contract of the library-authoring-qualification pack: one bounded local check that a
2: # Library Insight authoring-qualification source contract was present and valid.
3: #
4: # This pack invokes no Liberty file, no QuaLib, no edarun, no production Library fact, no E1--E4
5: # requalification and no customer data. It does not claim commercial qualification; the files it
6: # asserts its scope from are named under `knowledge:` below.
7: id: library-authoring-qualification
8: version: '1'
9: title: Library authoring-qualification probe
10: 
11: # What a Site binds, in its own site file under `bindings:`. The pack binds none of them.
12: inputs:
13:   - name: flowRoot
14:     description: >-
15:       The Golden Flow's root on the Site: the directory holding analyze-library-contract.sh,
16:       read-library-contract.py and the shipped input fixture library-input.json. Read-only to a
17:       Campaign — a generation runs on its own copy of it, never here.
18:   - name: workspaceRoot
19:     description: >-
20:       Where Campaign workspaces are created. The Site's Permit must allow writes under it; nothing
21:       this pack does writes anywhere else.
22: 
23: # What a generation leaves in its own Campaign workspace. The envelope is the artifact the reader
24: # reads; the reading itself is the typed value the reader emits from it.
25: outputs:
26:   - name: libraryContract
27:     path: flow/library-insight.json
28:     reader: library-contract
29:     description: >-
30:       The authoring-qualification envelope stage one of the flow wrote in this Campaign's copy of
31:       it, carrying the source identity, the fixed schema, the qualification label, the provenance
32:       and the explicit unknowns. The judged output. A generation that cannot produce a valid
33:       envelope produces no reading at all.
34: 
35: # The first word of every declared command line below: the tool's argv[0] and the reader's. The
36: # Site's Permit decides each one, and a word not here is refused before a Campaign starts. The
37: # reader's script runs python3 in turn — inside its own shell, exactly as the flow's second command
38: # line states — so python3 is not a wrapper of this pack and is not declared as one.
39: environment:
40:   wrappers:
41:     - sh
42: 
43: # What is copied out of flowRoot into <workspace>/flow/ once per Campaign: the flow's two stages and
44: # its own input fixture. The flow itself stays where it lies — this pack holds no copy of it.
45: workspace:
46:   copy:
47:     - analyze-library-contract.sh
48:     - read-library-contract.py
49:     - library-input.json
50: 
51: tools:
52:   - id: analyze-library-contract
53:     file: tools/analyze-library-contract.sh
54:     description: >-
55:       Stage one of the local Golden Flow, run inside the Campaign's own copy of it: check the five
56:       fields of the shipped input fixture and write the envelope the reader reads. An input missing
57:       any required field exits non-zero and writes no envelope, so no reading can exist for it.
58:     inputs: [WORKSPACE, INPUT_FIXTURE]
59:     argv:
60:       - sh
61:       - ${WORKSPACE}/flow/analyze-library-contract.sh
62:       - ${WORKSPACE}/flow/${INPUT_FIXTURE}
63:       - ${WORKSPACE}/flow/library-insight.json
64: 
65: # Every rule this pack's judge node may apply, by reference: this folder's rules/ first, the bundle's
66: # second. Both of these are this pack's own.
67: rules:
68:   - library-contract-nonnegative
69:   - library-contract-goal
70: 
71: # This pack's own domain knowledge, one entry per file, written for the purpose stated here.
72: knowledge:
73:   - file: scope-and-limits.md
74:     purpose: >-
75:       What this bounded local check establishes and what it must never be quoted as claiming.
76:   - file: reading-the-contract.md
77:     purpose: >-
78:       The five required fields, the fixed schema and label, the reader's gate, and the
79:       source-linked counterexamples with the refusal or typed value each must produce.
80: 
81: # The bound goal. This pack's target is fixed by business, not chosen per Campaign: the goal rule
82: # compares the reading against exactly one count, and the bounds below say so. A Campaign states the
83: # goal; it cannot widen or narrow it into a different question.
84: goal:
85:   library_contract_goal: { type: number, unit: count, min: 1, max: 1, default: 1 }
86: 
87: # The strategy of this pack, and the whole of it: one knob, with one legal value.
88: #
89: # A generation varies nothing, so the only thing a Run is set to is the identity of the input it
90: # reads — the flow's own shipped fixture, which the Campaign's copy of the flow carries. The option
91: # list holds that one name and no other, so no Run can ask a different question: a different input
92: # is a new Campaign, not another generation of this one. The knob is declared rather than left out
93: # because this harness's Strategy is what an Explore node chooses from, and an empty one would leave
94: # the node nothing to be set to.
95: strategy:
96:   inputFixture: { type: choice, options: [library-input.json], default: library-input.json }
97: 
98: # What a person reads each number under, for the faces that show it: one entry per goal parameter
99: # the graph binds, one per knob above. A choice states no unit, because a choice is measured in
100: # nothing.
101: words:
102:   library_contract_goal: { label: library contract reading at least, unit: count }
103:   inputFixture: { label: input fixture }

<type>file</type>

1: # The library-authoring-qualification probe as a HimaFabric graph. One generation, four nodes and
2: # no loop: run stage one of the flow, read the envelope it wrote, judge it with the constraint rule
3: # and then the goal rule, and complete the goal only when both passed.
4: #
5: # There is no revisit edge: this pack has no strategy knob, so no decision can open another
6: # generation. A different input is a new Campaign, not a second generation of this one.
7: id: library-authoring-qualification
8: version: '1'
9: entry: analyze
10: 
11: nodes:
12:   # Act: run the pack's tool on the Site, in the Campaign's own copy of the flow, and wait for it.
13:   # Only the strategy knob is chosen here — the name of the input fixture, whose one legal value is
14:   # the flow's own. WORKSPACE is the Run's own workspace, which the fabric already holds and a node
15:   # may not bind.
16:   - id: analyze
17:     kind: act
18:     parameters:
19:       tool: analyze-library-contract
20:       arguments:
21:         INPUT_FIXTURE: { from: strategy, name: inputFixture }
22: 
23:   # Act: read the envelope that generation produced into HimaLedger, through the contract's own
24:   # reader. When the flow refuses the input, or the envelope is not valid, this reading produces no
25:   # value at all — which is not a zero and never becomes one.
26:   - id: read-contract
27:     kind: act
28:     parameters:
29:       observes: libraryContract
30: 
31:   # Judge: the constraint rule first, then the goal rule whose bound goal the Run binds. The
32:   # outgoing edge is chosen by the outcome of the first rule listed — the constraint.
33:   - id: judge
34:     kind: judge
35:     parameters:
36:       rules:
37:         - library-contract-nonnegative
38:         - library-contract-goal
39:       bind:
40:         library_contract_goal: { from: goal, name: library_contract_goal }
41: 
42:   # Explore: the only place a Campaign of this pack can be ended as goal met, and only on the
43:   # constraint's PASS together with the goal's PASS. The chooser declares no next strategy, because
44:   # there is nothing to vary; any other combination matches no clause and reaches no goal-met
45:   # decision.
46:   - id: decide
47:     kind: explore
48:     parameters:
49:       chooser: library-contract-decide
50: 
51:   # Wait: where a Run stops for a person — a refused or absent reading, a constraint the flow
52:   # cannot produce, or a valid envelope that is not ready. Nothing draws an edge here from the
53:   # explore node and nothing needs to: a Hard blocker is routed to the graph's wait node by the
54:   # fabric itself, exactly as an UNDETERMINED the pack labelled no edge for is.
55:   - id: blocked
56:     kind: wait
57:     parameters:
58:       blocker: hard-blocker
59: 
60: edges:
61:   - { from: analyze, to: read-contract }
62:   - { from: read-contract, to: judge }
63:   # The constraint passed: the goal rule decides whether the Campaign is done, which is the
64:   # chooser's decision and not the edge's.
65:   - { from: judge, to: decide, outcome: PASS }
66:   # The constraint failed: a negative reading is a refusal, not a next experiment.
67:   - { from: judge, to: blocked, outcome: FAIL }
68:   # UNDETERMINED is left unlabelled on purpose: no reading exists, so no rule may pass.
